title: Triangular maximal tori in PGL2 are locally diagonal
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], and put $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $G=\operatorname{PGL}_{2,S}$ be the fppf sheaf quotient of the group of invertible $2\times2$ matrices by scalar invertible matrices; fppf coverings are faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. Write $B_\infty\subseteq G$ for the image of the upper triangular invertible matrices and $D\subseteq B_\infty$ for the image of the diagonal invertible matrices. Let $T\hookrightarrow B_\infty$ be a closed subgroup scheme [def-weil-closed-immersion] which is a maximal torus of $G$: it is fppf locally a finite product of copies of $\mathbf G_m=\operatorname{Spec}A[z,z^{-1}]$ and every geometric fibre is maximal among tori. All groups are schemes with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams [def-sc-group-scheme]. Define $Y$ as the sheaf whose sections on an $S$-scheme $V$ are the elements $b\in B_\infty(V)$ for which $bT_Vb^{-1}=D_V$ as subgroup functors on $V$-schemes. Then $Y$ is represented by a smooth surjective $S$-scheme and left multiplication by $D\simeq\mathbf G_{m,S}$ makes it a $D$-torsor: $(d,y)\mapsto(dy,y)$ identifies $D\times_SY$ with $Y\times_SY$, and sections exist etale locally on $S$. Moreover $Y$ has sections Zariski locally on $S$. In particular, there is a Zariski open cover $(S_i)$ and $b_i\in B_\infty(S_i)$ with $b_iT_{S_i}b_i^{-1}=D_{S_i}$, with the same identity after any base change.

source.place: Conrad, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124: the smooth transporter is a torsor under D, and multiplicative-group torsors are Zariski locally trivial. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this assertion in this form.

proof.text:
Use the matrix quotient of [lem-sfb-projective-frames-pgl]. An upper triangular invertible matrix has invertible diagonal entries. Dividing by its bottom-right entry gives a unique representative
$$b(a,x)=\begin{pmatrix}a&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad a\in R^\times,\ x\in R.$$
Scalar-invariance and uniqueness make these coordinates glue from local matrix representatives. Thus $B_\infty=\operatorname{Spec}A[a,a^{-1},x]$, with product $(a,x)(c,z)=(ac,az+x)$, and $D$ is $x=0$, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m$. This is an affine finite-type group; it is the principal open $a\ne0$ in $\mathbf A^2_S$, hence smooth by [sbc-lem-affine-space-smooth] and [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes]. For every commutative $S$-algebra $R$, conjugation of the universal diagonal element gives
$$b(a,x)\begin{pmatrix}t&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}b(a,x)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}t&x(1-t)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{over }R[t,t^{-1}].$$
If $b(a,x)$ normalizes $D$ as a subgroup functor, the coefficient of $t$ in $x(1-t)$ is zero, so $x=0$. Conversely $x=0$ centralizes $D$. This proves $N_{B_\infty}(D)=D$ on all test algebras and hence all test schemes, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124; matrix normalizer calculation and inclusion/equality clarification written out by Q29.

proof.text: Fix any geometric point $\bar s$ with algebraically closed residue field $F$. The chart in step 1 shows that $(B_\infty)_F$ is smooth, affine and of finite type. It is connected: $F[a,a^{-1},x]$ is a domain, so its zero prime is a point whose closure is the entire spectrum; every nonempty open contains that point, precluding a decomposition into two nonempty disjoint opens. The torus $D_F$ is maximal in this group: any torus containing it is commutative, hence lies in its centralizer, which step 1 identifies with $D_F$. The torus $T_F$ is maximal in this group because a strictly larger torus there would also be a strictly larger torus in $G_F$, contrary to the hypothesis. Apply [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] to the smooth connected group $(B_\infty)_F$ and these two maximal tori. It supplies $b_{\bar s}\in B_\infty(F)$ with $b_{\bar s}T_Fb_{\bar s}^{-1}=D_F$ as subgroup schemes.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124; matrix normalizer calculation and inclusion/equality clarification written out by Q29.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-transporter-smooth] to the smooth affine finite-type group $B_\infty$ of step 1 and its closed multiplicative-type subgroups $T,D$. They satisfy the multiplicative-type hypothesis since a product of multiplicative groups is $D_R(\mathbf Z^r)$, and $T$ has precisely such fppf local presentations by assumption. This gives a smooth closed scheme $Z\subseteq B_\infty$ representing the containment condition $bT_Vb^{-1}\subseteq D_V$. In fact this condition is equality. On any affine piece of an fppf cover splitting $T_V$, the resulting homomorphism $T_V\to D_V$ is, Zariski locally, induced by an integer character map $u:\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z^r$, by [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality]. On every geometric fibre it is an isomorphism: its source is a maximal torus in $G$ and is contained in the torus $D$, so it cannot be proper. The locally constant integer map $u$ must therefore be an isomorphism wherever the base is nonempty. Indeed after a geometric specialization it is the character map of an isomorphism, so $r=1$ and $u=1$ or $-1$. Thus the homomorphism is already an isomorphism before specialization on each such piece. The local inverse identifies the two subgroup functors, and equality of their sections descends along the splitting cover because both are fppf sheaves. Consequently $Z=Y$ as functors. This proves representability and smoothness for the equality transporter of the statement, without inferring an isomorphism of arbitrary schemes merely from their fibres.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124; matrix normalizer calculation and inclusion/equality clarification written out by Q29.

proof.text: Every geometric fibre of $Y\to S$ has the point $b_{\bar s}$ from step 2. Its image in $S$ is the underlying point $s$, so $Y\to S$ is surjective. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-space-cover-etale-sections] to this smooth surjection (a scheme is in particular an algebraic space). We obtain an etale covering $(S_i'\to S)$ and sections $y_i\in Y(S_i')$.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124; matrix normalizer calculation and inclusion/equality clarification written out by Q29.

proof.text:
Left multiplication by $d\in D(V)$ preserves $Y(V)$, since $(dy)T_V(dy)^{-1}=dD_Vd^{-1}=D_V$. Given $y_1,y_2\in Y(V)$, put $n=y_1y_2^{-1}$. Then $nD_Vn^{-1}=D_V$, so step 1 gives $n\in D(V)$. Hence
$$(y_1,y_2)\longmapsto(y_1y_2^{-1},y_2)$$
is an inverse, natural in every test scheme $V$, to $(d,y)\mapsto(dy,y)$. Both maps are induced by the group operations and the indicated subgroup factorizations; composing them gives the identity. Thus $D\times_SY\simeq Y\times_SY$. Together with the etale sections from step 4, this is exactly the asserted left $D$-torsor structure.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124; matrix normalizer calculation and inclusion/equality clarification written out by Q29.

proof.text: Restrict the represented sheaf $Y$ to the small etale site of $S$ and identify $D$ with the units sheaf using step 1. Step 5 and the local sections of step 4 make it a $\mathbf G_m$-torsor there. By [lem-sc-line-bundle-torsor] there is an invertible $\mathcal O_S$-module $\mathcal L$ whose sheaf of frames is equivariantly isomorphic to this restriction of $Y$. An invertible module is locally isomorphic to $\mathcal O_S$ by [def-sc-invertible-module]. Choose a Zariski cover $(S_i)$ and frames $e_i:\mathcal O_{S_i}\simeq\mathcal L|_{S_i}$. Their inverse images under the sheaf isomorphism are sections of $Y$ over the open schemes $S_i$, hence are actual $b_i\in B_\infty(S_i)$ satisfying $b_iT_{S_i}b_i^{-1}=D_{S_i}$. No claim that every line bundle over an affine scheme is globally trivial is used.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Proposition 4.2.7, final paragraph of proof, printed p.124; matrix normalizer calculation and inclusion/equality clarification written out by Q29.

proof.text:
For any base change $W\to S_i$ and any $W$-scheme $V$, the group laws and the equality of subgroup functors defining $b_i$ restrict to
$$(b_i|_V)T_V(b_i|_V)^{-1}=D_V.$$
Thus the same conjugacy identity holds after every base change, including nonreduced and empty ones. This gives the final assertion of the statement.

Containment becomes equality through character-duality: u from Z to Z^r is an isomorphism on geometric fibres, so r=1, u=±1, and equality descends along the fppf cover.
